Tetanus: Causes and How It Spreads For Everyone Sept. 10, 2026 Español Key points Tetanus spores from the environment enter the body through cuts or wounds. Tetanus doesn't spread from person to person. It is possible to have tetanus infection more than once. Prevent tetanus by staying up to date with vaccinations and seeking appropriate care after a wound. Causes Bacteria live in the environment Spores of Clostridium tetani are common in the environment, including soil, dust, and manure. The spores develop into bacteria when they enter the body. Common exposures The spores can get into someone's body through broken skin, usually through injuries. Tetanus bacteria are more likely to infect certain breaks in the skin, including: Wounds contaminated with dirt, feces (poop), or saliva (spit) Puncture wounds (wounds caused by an object, like a nail or needle) Injuries with dead tissue (e.g., burns, crush injuries, frostbite) Dead tissue is a concern because it can promote bacteria growth. pages.text: Thawing permafrost is threatening Svalbard's 'corpse point' | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE Thawing permafrost is threatening Svalbard's 'corpse point' Human bones and artifacts from the largest whalers’ graveyard in the archipelago are at risk of disintegrating. For centuries, the permafrost protected the graves of men who hunted whales in the Arctic. But coastal erosion and melting ice now threaten to decay their remains. Lise Loktu and Espen Olsen, Governor of Svalbard. By Kat Long Published July 28, 2026 More than 300 years ago, young men from all over Western Europe boarded ships bound for the Arctic. Under the unceasing light of polar summer, in a landscape of rock and ice, they hunted bowhead whales in the waters surrounding the Svalbard archipelago. The work was brutal; the wind unrelenting. Many never made it home. They were buried in whalers’ graveyards, fully dressed in their woolen jackets and knitted hats. Their shallow graves were marked with mounds of stones. Now, the permafrost that once kept the burials safely frozen is thawing. “The unique thing about these whalers is that they aren’t preserved anywhere else,” says Lise Loktu , a researcher at the Norwegian Institute for Cultural Heritage Research (NIKU) in Tromsø, Norway. In a paper published this past spring in PLOS One , she reported that climate change has helped damage the irreplaceable artifacts over the past four decades. pages.title: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms
pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

pages.text: The 'Clotilda,' the Last Known Slave Ship to Arrive in the U.S., Is Found Skip to main content The descendants of Cudjo Lewis and Abache (above) heard stories of the ship that tore their ancestors from their homeland and now the wreck of the Clotilda has been confirmed to be found in Alabama's Mobile River. Wikimedia Commons One hundred and fifty-nine years ago, slave traders stole Lorna Gail Woods ’ great-great grandfather from what is now Benin in West Africa. Her ancestor, Charlie Lewis, was brutally ripped from his homeland, along with 109 other Africans, and brought to Alabama on the Clotilda , the last known slave ship to arrive in the United States. Today, researchers confirmed that the remains of that vessel, long rumored to exist but elusive for decades, have been found along the Mobile River, near 12 Mile Island and just north of the Mobile Bay delta. “The excitement and joy is overwhelming,” says Woods, in a voice trembling with emotion. She is 70 years old now. But she’s been hearing stories about her family history and the ship that tore them from their homeland since she was a child in Africatown, a small community just north of Mobile founded by the Clotilda ’s survivors after the Civil War. The authentication and confirmation of the Clotilda was led by the Alabama Historical Commission and SEARCH Inc., a group of maritime archaeologists and divers who specialize in historic shipwrecks. Searchers thought that an object glinting on satellite images was the missing aviator's plane. But the reality is more quotidian. The latest search for Amelia Earhart's plane centered on Nikumaroro, a remote atoll in the South Pacific. The island is at the center of a theory that Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan could have survived as castaways. Library of Congress, Getty Images By Rachel Hartigan Published October 19, 2026 In satellite imagery of the remote Pacific island of Nikumaroro, a mysterious object lies submerged in its lagoon—the outline of something vaguely plane-shaped. Dubbed the “ Taraia Object ” after a nearby peninsula, it has tantalized researchers who believe Amelia Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan could have ended up on the remote atoll and survived as castaways. But it’s not a plane. It’s not even metal. Astronomers detect immense ripples in the fabric of space-time For the first time, scientists detected low-frequency gravitational waves moving through the galaxy. These cosmic ripples are likely the distant echoes of supermassive black holes interacting and merging many billions of light-years away. A consortium of international researchers discovered these cosmic waves by measuring tiny time variations in radio signals from pulsar stars. The findings suggest that there were far more behemoth black holes in the early universe than previously thought, and continuing to study this new type of gravitational wave could help unravel details about the origins of our universe and better explain the unseen substances and forces that power the cosmos. 2. pages.text: The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning - BBC Sport By Jessica Abrahams BBC World Service Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in. She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet. Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes. The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space. It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles. Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race. Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons. So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend? With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future. There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances. Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first . But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country. Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live. With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic. Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else. The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. In the foothills, access routes to the mines ran through an area called Nok. Over the years, with the exploitation of the mines and the local people who overwhelmingly provided the labor force, numerous fragments of ancient pottery came to light but were largely ignored. But not everything incinerates — and increasing amounts of debris are hurtling back toward Earth and landing in backyards and farm fields. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. Renowned for its distinctive skiing culture, Japan is the ultimate wish list destination for serious skiers and snowboarders. If you’re used to the slopes of Europe or North America, you’ll appreciate the small differences: in the menu at a mountain cafe, the particular etiquette of the onsen, or even the heated toilet seats; everything feels different in Japan. But the main claim to fame is its soft, lightweight and very consistent powder snow. Westerly winds whip off the Siberian tundra and scoop up moisture over the Sea of Japan, before dumping it as snow over the archipelago. Hemophilia is caused by missing clotting proteins that make it difficult for the body to stop bleeding. New medicines are now preventing most dangerous bleeds, while gene therapy may offer some patients years of protection after a single treatment. Steve Gschmeissner, Science Photo Library By Meryl Davids Landau Published October 7, 2026 When two of Sara Pavao’s sons were diagnosed with hemophilia soon after birth, she feared the blood-clotting disorder would limit their lives—or leave them disfigured. As young children, Kapono, now 18, and Duke, 13, bruised frequently. “They’d be black and blue down their shins, on their forearms, and even on their faces after bumping into things,” Pavao recalls. Today, the brothers surf six-foot waves near their home on Kauai, Hawaii, ride dirt bikes on the island’s trails, and practice jujitsu. Kapono also kickboxes and previously played baseball and skateboarded—activities that would have been unthinkable for many children with hemophilia just a few decades ago. By Mark Hay Published February 27, 2026 As a matter of pragmatism and genuine preference, cultures across the globe have long and storied histories of cooking with offal—a catch-all term for every part of an animal that isn’t a slab of muscle meat. Yet for all that history, over the last few decades, offal consumption has declined worldwide, says food scientist Carlos Álvarez, especially in developed countries like the United States. The crown’s harsh laws had backfired, reminding colonists that they were at the mercy of the whims of King George and his Parliament. Twelve of the Colonies sent delegates to Carpenters’ Hall, a brick building in central Philadelphia. Georgia declined to participate, wary of alienating the British as it faced threats from nearby Native American nations. East Florida and West Florida, then in the hands of the British, also did not participate. The First Continental Congress convened at Carpenters’ Hall in Philadelphia—a setting associated with common Americans—in September 1774 to debate how to respond to the Intolerable Acts that placed Massachusetts under military rule. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. Murder and Maya hieroglyphs make an unlikely combination, but the two came together one evening several years ago, deep in the rain forest of northern Guatemala. It happened at La Naya, soon after Scotsman Ian Graham and his party had arrived to draw and photograph inscriptions that had been reported at the remote ruin. They found much more than they bargained for. "I never thought Maya archeology would be that dangerous," Ian told me when I visited him at Harvard University's Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, "but I sometimes feel fortunate to be alive. The looters are quite serious about their business." At La Naya, Ian and his group had unwittingly interrupted a gang of men engaged in cutting apart an ancient stone monument. Later, as the archeologists were setting up camp, shots rang out and Pedro Arturo Sierra, one of Ian's assistants, fell dying. The shooting was an isolated incident. To Egyptologists, the Bahariya Oasis is known as the Valley of Golden Mummies, a necropolis where archaeologists have uncovered hundreds of gilded and decorated mummies dating back to the Greco-Roman era, roughly 2,000 years ago. But to paleontologists, the oasis is sacred because of something far older and far more legendary: Spinosaurus . The first ever specimen of this ferocious river monster was collected here more than a hundred years ago, along with fossils of several other enigmatic dinosaurs. Until they were lost forever, casualties of the World War II bombing that destroyed much of Munich. Swallowed by the flames, these dinosaurs essentially went extinct twice. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. pages.text: The eighth wonder of the ancient world may have an untouched tomb | National Geographic By Ángel Carlos Pérez Aguayo Published August 15, 2024 Atop Mount Nemrut lies what some call the eighth wonder of the world : a religious sanctuary of 10 colossal statues surrounding a mound believed to hold the tomb of an ancient king. These spectacular stone structures represent some of the most significant depictions of the religious and funerary practices of an ancient society that drew on both its Greek and Persian heritage. ( We know where the 7 wonders of the ancient world are—except for one. ) Located in a mountainous region of southeastern Turkey, Commagene was a province of the Hellenistic kingdom of Syria. When Alexander the Great died in 323 B.C., the Macedonian army general Seleucus I Nicator took control of the region. About 160 years later, a satrap (governor) called Ptolemaeus proclaimed himself king of Commagene, and the province broke away from the then crumbling Seleucid Empire. A new dynasty of Hellenistic sovereigns was born. In the first century B.C., Commagene formed a buffer zone between the Roman Republic and the Parthian Empire as they fought for control of Anatolia. During this time, Commagene enjoyed a golden era. The society was a blend of Greek and Persian culture; culture merging was common for the Hellenistic period. Between approximately 70 and 36 B.C., Commagene’s most famous king, Antiochus I, ruled. He tried to stay neutral in the conflict between the Romans and the Parthians. That new option, along with other injection-free medicines that have recently become available, could be especially consequential for people who fear needles. Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C. It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown. During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification. Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes. "It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. pages.text: The federal budget process | USAGov Skip to main content The federal budget process Learn about the federal government’s budget process. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. Proposed funding is divided among 12 subcommittees, which hold hearings. Each handles funding for different government functions such as defense spending or energy and water.
